item.text: {"question_id":"5B.3","answer":"For 2023, macroeconomic management was mixed. Mexico’s established framework, independent central bank, flexible exchange rate, and sound financial sector supported stability: GDP grew 3.2%, inflation declined to 5.5%, banks remained well-capitalized and liquid, the fiscal deficit was 4.3% of GDP, public debt 46.8% of GDP, and gross fixed investment grew 18.0% (BATCH-0016-E013; BATCH-0022-R02-E002; BATCH-0022-R02-E003; BATCH-0052-E019). The IMF credited the authorities’ policies and frameworks with restraining debt and containing inflation, but monetary stabilization was principally attributable to Banxico’s autonomous policy rather than personally to López Obrador; growth also reflected U.S. recovery, domestic demand, FDI, and nearshoring (BATCH-0016-E013; BATCH-0052-E019). Fiscal administration showed some favorable developments: tax-to-GDP reached 17.7% in 2023, while earlier administration reforms were associated by IMF staff with stronger revenue performance and lower estimated VAT evasion, though causal attribution was difficult to isolate (BATCH-0046-E005; BATCH-0017-E007). Against this, revenue remained low by OECD standards, fiscal reserves had fallen below 0.1% of GDP in the earlier pandemic period, and the IMF identified the need for deeper medium-term fiscal-rule and debt-anchor reforms; the evidence records proposed preparedness measures, not complete subsequent operation (BATCH-0046-E005; BATCH-0017-E003). The administration’s support for financially weak PEMEX and the 2024 budget proposal created forward-looking sustainability concerns: the IMF judged the proposed 2024 stance procyclical, with a projected 5.4% deficit, while the World Bank warned that PEMEX, pension, and social-program spending could crowd out education and infrastructure; these are 2024 projections or emerging risks, not realized 2023 outcomes (BATCH-0016-E015; BATCH-0052-E019). Financial-sector resilience coexisted with unresolved supervisory weaknesses, including gaps in regulatory autonomy, resources, consolidated supervision, and risk-based oversight, with attribution applying to authorities and regulators collectively rather than solely to the president (BATCH-0016-E020; BATCH-0052-E022; BATCH-0052-E024). Overall, the evidence supports credible short-run macroeconomic stability and implementation of some fiscal and monetary arrangements, but not an unqualified finding of ruler-controlled, fully durable
